tagline: A former footpath leads from Lake Superior to the border lakes.
intro: The Gunflint Trail winds 57 paved miles from Grand Marais on Lake Superior to Saganaga Lake near the Canadian border. A National Scenic Byway since 2009, it crosses the Superior National Forest. The Federal Highway Administration highlights Lake Superior views and a changing forest, from deciduous trees through conifers to boreal woods.

The route began as a footpath linking inland lakes with Lake Superior. Cook County widened it into a dirt road in the 1890s to support the Paulson Mine. Local business owners paid for improvements in the 1920s. In 1929, the road was extended north to Saganaga Lake to serve construction of Chik Wauk and Sea Gull lodges, tying its growth to tourism. By 1957, pavement reached Hungry Jack Lake from Grand Marais. The final gravel section, south of Sea Gull Lake, was paved in 1979.

From Highway 61 in Grand Marais, drive north to Northern Light Lake, then northwest along the Brule River. Beyond the river crossing, the road follows Swamper Creek and bends west along Poplar Lake, passing Birch, Mayhew and Loon lakes before the Gunflint Lake access roads. It turns north near Round Lake, then west at Sea Gull Lake to end at Saganaga. FHWA advises at least two hours for the trip, including the return along the same road.

moments.title: Pincushion Mountain
moments.text: Pincushion Mountain offers a view back toward the water the Gunflint Trail leaves behind. The peak belongs to the Sawtooth Mountains, beside the Lake Superior boundary of Cook County. From its summit, the view includes the mountain range, Lake Superior, and the town, harbor and lighthouse of Grand Marais.

moments.title: Hungry Jack Lake
moments.text: Hungry Jack Lake marked a stage in the gradual paving of the Gunflint Trail: by 1957, pavement extended here from Grand Marais. The lake covers 463 acres and reaches a maximum depth of 71 feet, at an elevation of 1,680 feet. The lake was putatively named for Anderson Jackson Scott, a surveyor's assistant temporarily without food supplies here.

moments.title: Saganaga Lake
moments.text: At Saganaga, the road reaches a lake shared by Minnesota and Ontario. Its name comes from an Ojibwe term meaning Lake of Many Islands. Most of the lake lies within the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, Quetico Provincial Park and La Verendrye Provincial Park. Overlooking it is Chik Wauk Lodge, a rough-cut stone building constructed in 1933 and used since 2010 as a museum and nature center. The lodge building has not been significantly altered since its original construction. The stone lodge was once the center of a fishing resort, offering cabins and meals as well as access to the lakes.
